newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine 1997 draft budget targets growth.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine 1997 draft budget targets growth.

text.p: Ukraine's 1997 draft budget envisages economic growth for the first time in the post-Soviet era and hopes to raise industrial enterprises from the dead, Finance Minister Valentyn Koronevsky said on Thursday.
But the ambitious plan is likely to face a tough ride through parliament, which has just approved a three-year economic growth programme.
"This budget wants to create economic growth in Ukraine next year," Koronevsky said as he delivered the draft, which he said was linked with the economic programme, to parliament.
He said Ukraine would follow a tight fiscal policy, curb spending and pay off its $1.7 billion wage backlog without spurring inflation.
But he also said the budget would face a rough time in parliament, which is dominated by leftist forces, and that figures could be changed before it is passed by 1997.
Budget committee chief Mykola Azarov said parliamentary deputies doubted the document's spending targets could be achieved and said the deficit figure was unrealistic.
"We believe we do not have to accept this budget in its current state -- we have to work on it and improve it," he said.
The draft budget foresees a 4.09 billion hryvnia deficit -- 3.8 percent of total GDP.
It sees 1997 yearly inflation at 24.9 percent, compared to government forecasts of 45 percent for 1996.
It also forecasts 1.7 percent growth in gross domestic product (GDP) and industrial output, and six percent growth in agricultural output, Economy Minister Vasyl Hureyev said.
"Next year Ukraine will see the start of economic growth," he said.
Over half of the budget deficit would be covered by internal funding, while foreign credits and planned Eurobond issues would make up the rest.

Koronevsky said Kiev would issue four billion hryvnia in Treasury bills in 1997. It would spend 3.3 billion from the issues just to service 1996 issues, while the remainder would help plug the deficit.
The former Soviet republic's GDP plunged 11.8 percent last year, and September year-on-year industrial production fell nine percent.
The budget sees the new hryvnia currency, which stood at 1.777 to the dollar on the Ukraine Interbank Currency Exchange, at 1.9 hryvnia to dollar by end of 1997.
Central bank chief Viktor Yushchenko told reporters he supported the budget and repeated earlier promises not to print money to cover spending shortfalls.
"The 1997 budget and its policies are aimed at having a strong and healthy hryvnia," he said.
He said acceptance of the budget would form the central condition for issue of Ukraine's first Eurobond next year.
